I assume a random person approaching me with a line is looking for a casual encounter, not a serious relationship. If I'm mistaken, it's not a big deal since I'm not actively seeking to date. However, I don't see how a stranger could pursue a meaningful relationship with another stranger. I'm not into casual encounters, so I'll usually decline their advances - even if they are attractive. I'm polite about it, as I'm a social person and they haven't done anything wrong by approaching me. I just don't engage with or share my contact information with strangers.

The "cleverness" of their approach plays a role in that it's unexpected and charming, which I find appealing. If nothing else, it makes me want to engage in conversation with them, to see what they're like, and to discover if they're as playful as their line suggests. In other words, that interaction piques my interest. Does physical attraction matter? Absolutely. If they're only interested in a casual encounter, would I still decline? Not sure, probably. If they're looking for a date or my contact information, am I interested? If the conversation flows well...yes, I am.

So, it "works on me" in that it prompts me to reconsider automatically shutting them down. After all, they weren't what I expected. And they *listened*. They took the time to respond to what I said. I appreciate that...so I'm curious about them, especially if there's physical chemistry.

**TL;DR: I tend to politely decline advances from strangers because I'm not into casual encounters, and I assume that's what they're after. So in most situations, they don't have a chance even if they're attractive. Unexpected cleverness makes me reconsider and engage in conversation, though physical attraction determines if it goes any further. So it "works" because it creates an opportunity where there was none.**

Side note, discussing it in this "I'm passive/they approach/I decide" manner feels a bit egotistical, even if that's the scenario, so I want to clarify that I do take the initiative as well! For what it's worth, I also appreciate a simple "hey, I'm [name]," but it doesn't spark a conversation as easily as this approach does.

When nitrites are exposed to high heat, in the presence of amino acids, they can turn into compounds called nitrosamines.

There are many different types of nitrosamines… and most of them are potent carcinogens. 

Because most processed meats tend to be high in sodium nitrite and they’re high protein foods (a source of amino acids), exposing them to high heat creates the perfect conditions for nitrosamine formation.

It’s important to keep in mind that nitrosamines mostly form during very high heat. Even though vegetables also contain nitrates/nitrites, they are rarely exposed to such high heat.

I guess if you only ever flame your vegetables on the barbecue, you might have cause for concern. But most people don't cook high-nitrate vegetables like lettuce, spinach, beets, or celery on high heat (or at all)... processed meats, on the other hand, are pretty popular.

And yes, nitrosamines are considered unhealthy since many are carcinogenic.

It's the combination of high heat and amino acids, actually (I replied to this same individual earlier in the thread with more information if you want to look for it.) 

Nitrates themselves are fine; it's what they can turn into that's the problem.

Make a list of all your good qualities - not just the materialistic stuff you listed here, but your interests, aspects of your personality, and anything else you bring to the table. Forget dating individuals for a moment and just list why someone would want to be your friend. Then read that list to yourself before going on a date.

In terms of being a pet rock on the date, maybe change your approach. Now you know you need to be more engaged so that's the first part. The "how" is tricky, but it seems like you clam up because you put pressure on yourself. Try walking into the date as if you're having coffee with a good friend. If that's asking too much, keep it simple: smile, greet them warmly, and immediately jump into conversation. It can be as simple as asking how their week went. If the conversation lags, don't default to an interrogation or silence. Instead, say, "hey, random question" then ask an icebreaker like "where would you go if you could fly anywhere in the world right now?" to open a new line of conversation. If neither of you are into travel, food, or culture I suggest you find your own question though lol. The point is, you should try and treat a date as a low-pressure experiment. See if that's something that works for you. Bonus, this "friends" approach is usually very refreshing and disarming since most people do date interview questions, so keep the general concept in mind even if you become more confident. Just remember: you should aim to each talk 50% of the time. No one can connect with you if you're not giving them something to work with.

Also, since I've already jumped into giving tons of advice I'd may as well add one more point...stop assuming you're "a thing"/a couple just from the first date. Although, even if you were, why would you then stop trying to relate to her? Relationships where one person stops trying...fail. The reality is that it'll always take work. More than that, this assumption is a pretty lousy one because everyone wants to be wanted. If you don't put in any effort because you assume you're "a thing" (whatever that means), you're not showing any signs you're actually interested in that date. No one will want to be with you if they think you're settling for them instead of actually wanting them. So yes, you absolutely need to converse and interact with them - no "I guess" about it.

I hope some of that was helpful. You sound pretty nice in your different replies here actually, just really inexperienced. So treat your next few dates as practice, and make a point of (a) remembering why their interest in you is legitimate and (b) using an 'already friends' approach to take the pressure off, engage more/talk 50% of the time, and give dates a way to connect. Good luck!

The ring should resemble something she would genuinely wear, rather than something that might not suit her taste. It would be unfortunate if she never wore it because it didn't align with her style. Consider the metal choice carefully. Some individuals, like myself, may not wear certain types of gold. The same likely applies to other metal options.
